content: The Pap smear, also known as the Papanicolaou test, is a gynecological screening procedure developed by Georgios Papanikolaou. Its primary purpose is to detect premalignant and malignant changes in the ectocervix. Additionally, it can identify infections and abnormalities in the endocervix and endometrium, although it is not specifically designed for these purposes. The test involves collecting cells from the outer opening of the cervix and the endocervix to identify abnormalities, including dysplasia or cervical intraepithelial neoplasia, which are often caused by human papillomavirus (HPV) infections. The ultimate goal of the Pap smear is to detect and prevent the progression of HPV-induced cervical cancer and other abnormalities in the female reproductive tract. The procedure for obtaining a Pap smear sample involves using a device, such as an Aylesbury spatula or a plastic-fronded broom, to collect cells from the cervix. These cells are then placed on a glass slide or into a liquid medium for laboratory analysis. The sample is stained using the Papanicolaou technique, which employs specific dyes to highlight cellular features. A trained cytotechnologist examines the sample under a light microscope to identify any abnormalities. In cases of abnormal findings, the sample is further reviewed by advanced practitioners or pathologists. The sensitivity of conventional cytology is approximately 72%, while its specificity is around 94%. Liquid-based cytology, introduced in the mid-1990s, involves placing the collected sample into a vial containing a liquid medium, typically ethanol-based, which preserves the cells. This method allows for the creation of a thin-layer preparation for microscopic examination and facilitates HPV testing. Liquid-based cytology has been shown to reduce the rate of unsatisfactory specimens and has sensitivity and specificity rates ranging from 61% to 66% and 82% to 91%, respectively. Abnormal Pap smear results are categorized using the Bethesda system. These include squamous cell abnormalities, such as atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (LSIL), high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions (HSIL), and squamous cell carcinoma. Glandular cell abnormalities, such as atypical glandular cells not otherwise specified (AGC-NOS), can also be identified. While the Pap smear is effective in detecting cervical abnormalities, it is not highly sensitive for detecting infections like yeast, herpes simplex virus, or trichomoniasis. The effectiveness of the Pap smear in reducing cervical cancer mortality is significant when combined with regular screening and appropriate follow-up. It is estimated that the test can reduce cervical cancer deaths by up to 80%. However, failures in prevention can occur due to irregular screening, inadequate follow-up of abnormal results, or errors in sampling and interpretation. In the United States, over half of invasive cervical cancers occur in women who have never undergone a Pap smear, and an additional 10-20% occur in women who have not had a Pap smear in the preceding five years. HPV testing has emerged as an important adjunct to Pap smear screening, particularly for women over the age of 30. High-risk HPV types, such as 16, 18, 31, and 45, are associated with an increased likelihood of developing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia. HPV testing has a sensitivity of 88% to 97% and a specificity of 73% to 93%, depending on the grade of cervical abnormalities being detected. The addition of HPV testing to Pap smear screening improves sensitivity but may reduce specificity, leading to an increased number of false-positive results and unnecessary follow-up procedures. Automated computer image analysis systems have been developed to assist in the screening of Pap smear samples. These systems aim to improve sensitivity and reduce the rate of unsatisfactory specimens. One such system has been approved by the FDA and is used in high-volume laboratories under human oversight. The Pap smear procedure involves the insertion of a speculum into the vagina to collect a sample from the cervix. The test is generally not scheduled during menstruation, as this can interfere with sample quality. While the procedure is typically only mildly uncomfortable, factors such as the patient's anatomy, the practitioner's skill, and psychological considerations can influence the level of discomfort. Results are usually available within three weeks, and minor side effects, such as slight bleeding or cramping, may occur after the procedure.
